summary.text: The Arctic oscillation is a ring-shaped seesaw of sea-level air pressure, with the Arctic north of 55° latitude on one side and a band near 37–45° N on the other.
When its index is positive, high pressure over the pole helps the jet stream blow strongly from west to east, keeping cold Arctic air locked up north.
When the index is negative, polar pressure drops, the winds weaken, and frigid polar air moves more freely into the middle latitudes.

facts.label: Southern counterpart
facts.value: Antarctic oscillation, or Southern Annular Mode

facts.label: Named in 1998
facts.value: By David W.J. Thompson and John Michael Wallace

facts.label: Forecast skill
facts.value: 7-day forecasts match observations at about 0.9 correlation

items.prompt: This winter, pressure over the Arctic is unusually high and the jet stream races steadily from west to east. What is the middle of North America most likely to get?

options.label: Repeated blasts of frigid Arctic air
A milder winter, with the cold held up north
Record snow from polar air spilling south
No change, since the pattern only affects the pole

items.explain: In the positive phase the strong west-to-east jet keeps Arctic air near the pole, so frigid air does not reach as far into the middle of North America.

items.prompt: Around the South Pole the matching pressure pattern is a nearly perfect circle, but around the North Pole the ring is lumpy. What breaks up the northern ring?

options.label: Stronger sunlight in the Arctic summer
Thicker sea ice than around Antarctica
Faster spin of the Earth near the North Pole
Continents and big landmasses in the north

items.explain: Large landmasses around the Arctic disrupt the ringlike structure, while the pattern around Antarctica stays nearly circular.

items.prompt: One February, three historic snowstorms hit the US mid-Atlantic, burying Baltimore twice. What was the Arctic oscillation index doing that month?

options.label: Sitting at its highest positive value on record
Resting near zero, in a neutral state
Sitting at its most negative value since 1950
Switching sign every few days all month

items.explain: In February 2010 the index hit its most negative monthly mean of the post-1950 era, and that month brought three separate historic mid-Atlantic snowstorms.

items.prompt: A friend says the Arctic oscillation flips on a fixed cycle, so you can read next winter's phase off a calendar. What is wrong with this?

options.label: It has no set period and wanders unpredictably
It flips every year, not on a longer cycle
It only changes once every few centuries
It follows the seasons, so it never varies

items.explain: The index varies with no particular periodicity and fluctuates randomly between negative and positive on daily to yearly time scales.

items.prompt: In the positive phase, higher pressure at midlatitudes pushes ocean storms farther north. Which places would you expect to turn wetter?

options.label: The Mediterranean and the western United States
Mexico and the Caribbean islands
Alaska, Scotland and Scandinavia
Central Africa and southern India

items.explain: With storms steered north, Alaska, Scotland and Scandinavia get wetter weather while the western United States and the Mediterranean dry out.

items.prompt: How does the North Atlantic oscillation relate to the Arctic oscillation?

options.label: A close relative; experts debate which is more basic
An unrelated pattern found in the tropical Pacific
The southern hemisphere version of the same ring
A pattern that replaced it after the 1970s

items.explain: The North Atlantic oscillation is a close relative of the Arctic oscillation, and there is debate over which one better represents the atmosphere's dynamics.
